title: api-gateway: tune streaming proxy buffers, routing precedence and payload limits (openai-compat + function-calling stability)
author: Avery Chen
release_notes: Improves streaming stability for function/tool-calling and large structured outputs by tuning proxy buffers and routing precedence; no user-facing API changes, but raises per-route default payload limits and returns early 413 for oversized requests.
description: Motivation: we saw increased incidents where streaming responses for function/tool-calling and large structured outputs would intermittently stall or truncate when proxied through the API gateway, especially for OpenAI-compatibility endpoints that emit frequent small SSE chunks. Root causes identified: (1) the streaming proxy had an overly-small write buffer and aggressive coalescing which created backpressure loops under bursty chunk patterns; (2) route matching precedence occasionally routed requests to cheaper model pools (low-memory variants) when function-calling headers were present, causing token truncation mid-stream; (3) there was no early rejection for oversized request payloads which allowed gateway workers to consume memory and amplify instability. This PR: (a) increases and parameterizes the streaming proxy write/read buffer sizes with sensible defaults tuned from production traces; (b) adds explicit backpressure-aware flush semantics so small SSE/chunked frames are forwarded promptly rather than coalesced; (c) bumps the routing precedence rules so endpoints with function-calling or tool headers prefer full-memory model pools and fall back only on explicit policy; (d) enforces per-route configurable payload_size_limit and rejects early with HTTP 413 + structured error to prevent worker OOM cascades; (e) updates the OpenAI compatibility layer to map chunking headers (Transfer-Encoding: chunked and x-openai-streaming-mode) and to preserve event boundaries for function-calling JSON messages. Summary of commits: commit 1: gateway: parameterize proxy buffer sizes and expose via config; commit 2: gateway: implement backpressure-aware flush behavior and tests; commit 3: routing: prefer function-capable pools for requests with function-calling headers; commit 4: api-compat: map streaming headers and preserve SSE boundaries; commit 5: tests: add e2e sim for bursty chunked streams; commit 6: docs: update api-gateway config docs and openai-compat notes. Files changed (high level): - redwood/gateway/proxy/streaming.go (buffer tuning, flush semantics) - redwood/gateway/config/config.go (new proxy_buffer_{read,write}, default payload_size_limit) - redwood/gateway/routing/matcher.go (route precedence for function-calling) - redwood/openai-compat/streaming_mapper.go (preserve SSE boundaries, map headers) - redwood/openai-compat/tests/e2e_streaming_test.go (synthetic bursts) - redwood/docs/api-gateway.md (config docs) - redwood/tests/load/proxy_buffer_burst_sim.yaml (load sim) Small illustrative snippets: - streaming.go (flush): "if len(chunk) > 0 { w.write(chunk); if proxyConfig.flush_small_chunks { w.flush() } }" - matcher.go (precedence): "if req.Headers.Has(\"x-openai-function-calling\") { preferPool = poolSelector.FullMemoryFirst() }" Tests and metrics: added unit tests covering flush/no-flush behavior; added an e2e that simulates 10k small chunks at 30ms intervals and verifies end-to-end latency and no stalls. On internal perf lab, default config reduces median end-to-end stall incidents by ~92% and 99th-token-latency by ~30% on function-calling workloads. CI and rollout: initial CI run failed on a flake in e2e timing; fixed race by using deterministic tick driver in tests; final CI: all checks passing (lint, unit, integration, e2e). Rollout strategy: feature flagged; default-on in staging for 48h; canary rollout to 10% production traffic for 24h, monitor token-stall-rate and gateway memory; automatic rollback on >1% increase in p99 token-latency. Backwards compatibility and compatibility notes: no breaking changes to public API; OpenAI compatibility layer preserves semantics but tightens streaming boundaries which may cause some clients that relied on arbitrary coalescing to see different chunk sizes (these clients should be resilient). Request size rejections will return 413 with structured JSON: {"error":"request_too_large","max_bytes":<n>}. Review conversation (high level): - Diego Martinez (reviewer): "Thanks — this looks good overall. Two asks: add a config knob with a sane max so we can revert memory quickly, and please add a small benchmark for SSE coalescing edge-cases." - Avery Chen (author): "Added proxy_config.max_buffer_bytes and included a synthetic SSE coalescing benchmark in tests; see e2e_streaming_test.go." - Priya Kapoor (reviewer): "Router change is sensible, but please add telemetry counters when we forced-prefer function-capable pools so we can measure fallback rate." - Avery Chen: "Added gateway.metrics.counter('routing.prefer_function_pool') and increment on prefer path; added docs note." - Samir Rao: "Approving after CI fix. Confirmed canary plan and alerting thresholds." Merge details: merged via squash on 2026-02-22 by Diego Martinez. Post-merge actions: created a follow-up task (ENG-4897) to audit Dedicated capacity autoscaling interactions with increased buffer defaults; added a post-deploy dashboard for token-stall-rate and routing.fallback_rate. Notes about observability: added tracing span "gateway.proxy.flush" and new metric "gateway.proxy.flush_count" to understand flush frequency. Operational playbook: if memory climbs above expected after rollout, set proxy_buffer_write=64kb and proxy_buffer_read=64kb via remote config and monitor. Known limitations and future work: - Still seeing rare stalls for extremely high-fanout function callers; next step is to implement hierarchical proxy workers for per-connection isolation. - Consider exposing per-route stream_chunk_hint to help clients align chunk boundaries. Impact: addresses several customer incidents around function-calling truncation and streaming stalls; improves OpenAI-compat streaming behavior; low-risk rollout behind flags and with monitoring.
